items.title: Engineer reports working more despite AI tools reducing individual task effort, citing increased task volume and context switching in 2026
items.originalTitle: AI promised less work. I've never worked more
items.summary:
An engineer who uses AI agents extensively for software development finds that while individual tasks are easier, the overall workload has increased significantly in 2026 compared to previous years. The engineer's GitHub activity data shows a return to high contribution levels similar to their busiest coding years, despite holding a leadership role with less direct feature work.

The increased workload is attributed to managing multiple AI agents simultaneously, each requiring intermittent attention and causing frequent context switching, which is mentally draining. This shift has led to more tasks being undertaken and a heavier, more fragmented work experience, challenging the initial promise that AI would reduce work hours.

items.title: Roblox crawled and downloaded 145GB of 3D models from multiple sites without permission, including adult content, likely for AI training [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Roblox downloaded 145GB models from us (including adult content) without asking
items.summary:
In October 2026, a crawler identifying as Roblox accessed nearly every project on Open3DLab, SFMLab, and SmutBase, downloading 1,027 files totaling 145.5GB, including adult content, without respecting robots.txt or terms of service. The crawler operated from an AWS IP and used a user agent linked to a Roblox researcher involved in 3D foundation model development. Site operators blocked the crawler after discovery and contacted Roblox, which did not respond.

The downloaded content included many projects licensed for non-commercial use only, raising concerns about unauthorized data use. Roblox has been developing a 3D foundation model called Cube since 2025, and this data collection appears related to that effort. The crawler resumed attempts after initial blocking but was consistently denied access. The incident highlights tensions around data scraping for AI training and the need for clearer permissions and communication between platforms and content creators.

items.title: Analysis: The Mythical Man-Month principle persists in AI development as adding more AI agents without clear coordination can slow progress [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Mythical Man-Month in the Age of AI
items.summary:
A recent analysis revisits Frederick P. Brooks Jr.'s 1975 Mythical Man-Month law, which states that adding manpower to a late software project makes it later, in the context of AI agents and large language models. While AI agents can onboard instantly and work continuously, the fundamental bottlenecks of sequential tasks and coordination overhead remain, now shifted to managing AI agents rather than people.

The article argues that without clear orchestration and well-defined requirements, adding multiple autonomous AI agents to a project can lead to inefficiencies such as conflicting changes and hallucinations, effectively producing incorrect results faster. This suggests that Brooks's Law still applies in the AI era, emphasizing the need for human oversight and precise project management to harness AI effectively.

items.title: Anthropic says feedback submitted via thumbs up/down buttons may be used to train models, storing related conversations for up to five years [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Giving chat feedback gives Anthropic your data
items.summary:
Anthropic states that inputs and outputs from its commercial products like Claude for Work and the Anthropic API are not used for model training by default. However, if users explicitly submit feedback or bugs through the thumbs up/down buttons or allow data use, their conversations and coding sessions may be stored and used for training purposes.

Feedback data includes the entire related conversation but excludes raw content from connectors unless copied directly into the chat. Anthropic de-links feedback from user and customer IDs before use and may retain this data for up to five years. Team or enterprise plan owners can disable feedback submission through organization settings to control data sharing.

The company is experimenting with different release approaches involving external academic collaborators to help interpret and validate the results, aiming to foster transparency and independent understanding.

For the mathematics discovery, OpenAI publicly released the AI-generated proof and formalization, allowing researchers to organize their own efforts. In computer science, an external group is collaborating to explain the result while making AI outputs publicly available. For physics, collaborators are preparing write-ups before releasing AI-produced materials. OpenAI emphasizes voluntary participation, transparency, and recognition for collaborators without seeking academic credit.

These approaches aim to balance expert involvement and open access, with OpenAI inviting feedback to improve the process and broaden participation in understanding these AI-generated scientific contributions.

The evolving landscape suggests that future software ownership will rely more on knowing when to intervene rather than hands-on coding.

This contrasts with a $1.6 billion loss in the same period a year earlier and challenges skepticism about the profitability of pay-as-you-go AI business models.

items.originalTitle: UK Home Office May Face Investigation Over Use of OpenAI Tools
items.summary:
A UK government watchdog is considering investigating the Home Office's use of AI tools based on OpenAI's GPT-4 to assist in processing asylum applications, following concerns about the tools' accuracy and the government's lack of transparency. The Independent Chief Inspector of Borders and Immigration is reviewing information from the Open Rights Group, which found higher error rates and no quality control in some AI-generated summaries used in asylum decisions.

The Home Office uses these AI tools to summarize interview transcripts and search asylum policy information to speed up case reviews, aiming to reduce a backlog of around 100,000 cases. However, critics including lawmakers and researchers warn that inaccuracies and cultural biases in the AI outputs could lead to unfair or harmful decisions, especially given the high stakes involved in asylum claims. The Home Office maintains that AI tools assist but do not replace human decision-makers and commits to ongoing monitoring and evaluation of their performance.

items.originalTitle: Stanford Study: Give up AI for a month for $500?
items.summary:
A Stanford working paper measures the consumer welfare gains from generative AI tools like ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and Copilot in the US by surveying willingness to accept compensation for giving up AI access for a month. The study found that average willingness to accept increased from $98 in 2025 to $124.50 in 2026, with the median rising from $3.40 to $11.40, alongside growth in the user base from 98 million to 115 million adults.
The researchers concluded that aggregate consumer surplus from generative AI substantially exceeds estimated revenues, indicating that consumers capture most of the welfare benefits. Usage frequency, workplace use, and paid subscriptions were key factors influencing valuations, with additional variation by demographics. The findings suggest generative AI is generating significant and rapidly growing welfare gains even before full productivity and GDP effects are reflected in official statistics.

items.originalTitle: Anthropic, SpaceX and Meta Cash Grabs
items.summary:
If it feels like it’s getting stuffy, that’s because the AI industry’s biggest names are doing their best to suck all the air out of the room. On Monday, Anthropic, SpaceX and Meta Platforms all unveiled their respective plans for raising gobs of cash to fund their AI ambitions, which could collectively add up to almost a quarter of a trillion dollars, while the getting is still good. This isn’t going to make it any easier for the weaker AI players, especially struggling neoclouds, to find fresh air to breathe in the form of capital.  

The biggest headline grabber of the day, of course, was Anthropic’s S-1 filing for its initial public offering. You can read a comprehensive breakdown of the most interesting details in that filing by my colleagues here. Anthropic didn’t say in its paperwork how much it plans to raise, though Reuters has previously reported that figure could be as much as $100 billion.

On Monday, Meta announced it has its sights set on a similar figure, as much as $95 billion through stock offerings. This wasn’t a surprise: Meta had telegraphed that a fundraising was in the offing as part of its recent third-quarter earnings report. In a filing last week, Meta made it clear it planned to move expeditiously to do the fundraising in part due to a congested pipeline of recent and future deals from the likes of Alphabet, SpaceX, Anthropic and OpenAI. A committee of Meta’s board, the filing said, “recognized that timing is important to secure capital before competitors saturate various funding options.”

But perhaps the most intriguing fundraising effort of the three companies was SpaceX’s $40 billion financing agreement with an entity managed by Apollo Global Management, through which the company will lease graphics processing units for its data centers. It’s the largest GPU financing in history, SpaceX said. My colleague Alex Eichenstein hears that the funding will happen through a special purpose vehicle that will be off SpaceX’s balance sheet, an arrangement that could help SpaceX avoid any negative impact on its credit rating.    

What makes the deal so interesting is that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk over the weekend, in a post on X teasing the $40 billion financing, used it as an opportunity to gloat over the reckoning he sees coming for his rivals. Musk said debt markets in recent weeks have closed to companies that don’t have revenue other than from AI data centers. “That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation,” he wrote. “Some will make it through, but not many.”

Musk’s argument is a self-serving one, of course: If he can help nudge already shaky neoclouds into the abyss, that could leave more capital for SpaceX and other big brands to tap in the future. The risk for Musk is that at some point investor disfavor spreads from neoclouds to bigger AI companies like his own. That could happen if AI customers start to lose patience with a lack of payoff from the technology. 

Over the weekend, the chief economist for Apollo—the same firm arranging SpaceX’s record-breaking GPU financing—published a sobering essay that pointed to business customers’ growing scrutiny of AI investments. “Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech,” the economist, Torsten Slok, wrote.

Microsoft’s Buyouts

Microsoft’s announcement on Monday of a new round of voluntary buyouts for employees had an eye-popping number attached to it: 60,000 employees, more than a quarter of its global workforce of 223,000, will be eligible for the offer. The actual number of Microsoft employees who take the company up on the offer is likely to be significantly lower, though, in part because the job market for tech industry employees is tight now.

My colleague Aaron Holmes is hearing that Microsoft is expecting a smaller percentage of employees to take the buyout than took advantage of a similar offer earlier this year. During that earlier round, about a third of the 9,000 employees Microsoft extended the buyout offer to actually accepted it. That suggests Microsoft believes fewer than 20,000 employees will take the latest buyout offer—a big number, to be sure, but one that doesn’t represent a dramatic thinning of the company’s ranks. 

In Other News

  • DoorDash is in advanced talks to acquire Instacart for $17 billion. On Friday, The Information first reported that Instacart was exploring a sale of the company and that it had held preliminary talks with DoorDash and Uber. 
  • Cathedral, a startup founded by former members of the Department of Government Efficiency, said it gained access to Anthropic’s internal systems using AI agents.
